title: Thalamic Reticular Neurons
intro: The thalamic reticular nucleus (TRN) is a thin sheet of GABAergic neurons wrapped around the thalamus like a shell. Every axon running between thalamus and cortex, in either direction, passes through it and leaves a collateral there, and TRN neurons send their inhibition back only to the thalamus. They are the pacemakers of sleep spindles and a candidate mechanism for attention, the 'guardian of the gateway' to cortex.

items: Morphology: fusiform or multipolar GABAergic cells with dendrites oriented along the sheet; axons project inward to the thalamic relay nuclei (and to other TRN cells via collaterals in some species). All TRN neurons express parvalbumin; subsets differ in calbindin and somatostatin and in whether they innervate first-order or higher-order nuclei (Clemente-Perez et al. 2017; Martinez-Garcia et al. 2020; Li et al. 2020).

Organisation: sectors for each sensory modality and motor/limbic domain, each roughly matched to the thalamic nucleus and cortical area it sits between, so the TRN forms a map of thalamocortical channels.

Inputs: excitatory collaterals from thalamocortical relay axons and from layer 6 corticothalamic axons (the latter very numerous and strong onto TRN cells), plus inputs from basal forebrain, brainstem and amygdala.

Firing: tonic firing when depolarised, and strong, long bursts when released from hyperpolarisation, from a dendritic T-type calcium current (Cav3.2/3.3) and SK potassium channels that make the bursts rhythmic (Huguenard & Prince 1992; Cueni et al. 2008).
Coupling: TRN cells are electrically coupled by gap junctions (Landisman et al. 2002), and in some species inhibit each other chemically, which helps synchronise them.

Sleep spindles: during light sleep, a TRN burst inhibits many relay cells; when the inhibition ends, the relay cells rebound-burst through their T-current and re-excite the TRN, which bursts again. This loop produces the 7 to 14 Hz waxing-and-waning spindles seen in EEG. An isolated TRN can generate spindle-frequency rhythms in vivo (Steriade et al. 1987).

Attentional gating: Crick (1984) proposed the TRN as an attentional 'searchlight'. Halassa et al. (2014) found TRN subnetworks whose activity depends on brain state, and Wimmer et al. (2015) found in mice that prefrontal cortex, through a pathway involving the basal ganglia, adjusts visual TRN activity to suppress the sensory channel that is not being attended.
Feedback inhibition and contrast: TRN inhibition of relay cells sharpens their responses in time and can switch them between tonic and burst mode.

Destexhe, Contreras, Sejnowski and Steriade (1994) and Destexhe et al. (1996): single- and multi-compartment HH-type TRN models with dendritic T-current, used with TC cells to reproduce spindles. The Destexhe models remain the standard building blocks.
Golomb, Wang and Rinzel (1994): an isolated TRN network model producing spindle-like synchronised oscillations through GABA-A and GABA-B coupling.
Bazhenov et al. (2002) and Hill and Tononi (2005): TRN cells in thalamocortical networks of sleep and waking.
Iavarone et al. (2023): Blue Brain's detailed thalamoreticular model of mouse somatosensory thalamus, with reconstructed TRN and TC cells, reproducing spindles and sensory responses.

Point-neuron versions: Izhikevich LTS-like or rebound-bursting parameters; the integrate-and-fire-or-burst model with TRN parameters (Smith et al. 2000 style); and in large models (Izhikevich & Edelman 2008) a simplified TRN population.

blocks.text: What this means for your SNN

items: If you add a thalamus, add a TRN-like inhibitory population that receives collaterals from both relay cells and layer 6, and inhibits only relay cells.
Give it rebound-bursting cells and slow (GABA-B) as well as fast inhibition if you want sleep-like rhythms; a TRN without bursting will not produce spindles.
A top-down signal that excites one TRN sector suppresses that sensory channel: this is the simplest biologically grounded attention mechanism for a multi-input column model.
